Pathology-05.question: ১) Which of the following is the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is H. pylori infection. Helicobacter pylori infection is the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) worldwide. It causes chronic gastritis, impaired mucosal defence, and increased susceptibility to acid-related injury.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • NSAIDs – A major cause of PUD, especially in elderly patients, by inhibiting COX enzymes → decreased prostaglandin synthesis → reduced mucus and bicarbonate secretion. However, overall H. pylori remains the most common cause.

  • Smoking – Increases the risk of ulcer formation and delays healing but is not the primary cause.

  • Alcohol – Can irritate gastric mucosa and worsen symptoms but is not a major cause of PUD.

High-yield points:

Major causes of peptic ulcer disease:

  1. H. pylori infection

  2. NSAID use

H. pylori association:

  • Duodenal ulcer

  • Gastric ulcer

  • Gastric adenocarcinoma risk

  • MALT lymphoma risk

NSAID mechanism:
COX inhibition → ↓ prostaglandins → ↓ mucus/bicarbonate + ↓ mucosal protection → ulcer formation

Pathology-05.question: ২) Gastric ulcer most commonly occurs in which of the following site?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is lesser curvature. The most common site of a gastric ulcer is the lesser curvature of the stomach, particularly near the incisura angularis and the junction of the body and antrum.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Body of stomach – Gastric ulcers may occur here but it is not the most common site.

  • Greater curvature – Uncommon site for gastric ulcer; lesions here raise suspicion of malignancy.

  • Fundus of stomach – Rare site for typical peptic ulcer disease.

High-yield points:

Common sites of peptic ulcers:

  • Gastric ulcer → Lesser curvature (near incisura angularis)

  • Duodenal ulcer → First part of duodenum (duodenal bulb)

Clinical pearl:

  • Ulcers on the greater curvature are less common and require careful evaluation for gastric cancer.

Pathology-05.question: ৩) Regarding H.pylori, which one is correct?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is comma shaped. Helicobacter pylori is a Gram-negative, curved (comma or S-shaped) bacillus that colonizes the gastric mucosa.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Gram positive – Incorrect. H. pylori is Gram-negative.

  • Non motile – Incorrect. H. pylori is motile due to its flagella, which help it penetrate the gastric mucus layer.

  • Multiple flagella – Incorrect. H. pylori has multiple unipolar flagella (a tuft of flagella at one pole), but in standard exam descriptions it is not usually described simply as "multiple flagella" compared with the characteristic curved shape.

High-yield points:

Helicobacter pylori:

  • Gram-negative curved bacillus

  • Comma/S-shaped

  • Motile with multiple unipolar flagella

  • Urease positive

  • Colonizes gastric antrum

  • Associated with:

    • Duodenal ulcer

    • Gastric ulcer

    • Gastric adenocarcinoma

    • MALT lymphoma

Key test association:

  • Rapid urease test → detects urease enzyme produced by H. pylori

  • Urea breath test → non-invasive confirmation of active infection

Pathology-05.question: ৪) Which of the following is the most common type of gastric malignancy?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is adenocarcinoma. Gastric adenocarcinoma is the most common malignant tumour of the stomach, accounting for the vast majority of gastric cancers. It arises from the gastric mucosal epithelial cells.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Squamous carcinoma – Very rare in the stomach because squamous epithelium is normally absent.

  • Transitional carcinoma – Typically arises in organs lined by transitional epithelium, such as the urinary tract, not the stomach.

  • Anaplastic carcinoma – Describes a poorly differentiated tumour pattern and is not the commonest gastric malignancy.

High-yield points:

Common gastric malignancies:

  • Adenocarcinoma → most common

  • Gastric lymphoma

  • Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)

  • Neuroendocrine tumour

Risk factors for gastric adenocarcinoma:

  • H. pylori infection

  • Chronic atrophic gastritis

  • Intestinal metaplasia

  • Smoking

  • Pernicious anaemia

Important association:

  • H. pylori → gastric adenocarcinoma + MALT lymphoma

Pathology-05.question: ৫) Which of the following is the most common GIT carcinoma?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is carcinoma of colon. Among gastrointestinal (GIT) malignancies, colorectal carcinoma is the most common overall. In many exam contexts, colon carcinoma is used as the representative answer.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ca oesophagus – Common in certain geographical regions but not the most common GIT carcinoma overall.

  • Ca rectum – A major component of colorectal cancer but less common than colon when considered separately.

  • Ca stomach – Previously one of the most common GIT cancers worldwide, but overall incidence has declined.

High-yield points:

Most common GIT carcinoma → Colorectal carcinoma

Most common gastric malignancy → Adenocarcinoma

Most common oesophageal malignancy (global) → Squamous cell carcinoma
Most common oesophageal malignancy in Western countries → Adenocarcinoma

Pathology-05.question: ৬) Which of the following is the tumor marker of for pancreatic cancer?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is CA 19-9. CA 19-9 is the most commonly used tumour marker associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma. It is mainly useful for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence, rather than screening, because it lacks sufficient sensitivity and specificity.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • AFP – Associated mainly with hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac tumours.

  • Beta-hCG – Associated with gestational trophoblastic disease and germ cell tumours.

  • CA 125 – Associated mainly with ovarian epithelial carcinoma and is also used in monitoring ovarian cancer.

High-yield points:

Important tumour markers:

  • Pancreatic carcinoma → CA 19-9

  • Hepatocellular carcinoma → AFP

  • Colorectal carcinoma → CEA

  • Ovarian carcinoma → CA 125

  • Prostate carcinoma → PSA

  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma → Calcitonin

Pathology-05.question: ৭) Which of the following is the microscopic finding of gastric adenocarcinoma?
৮) Which of the following is the most common Cause of acute upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is peptic ulcer disease (PUD). Peptic ulcer disease is the most common cause of acute upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage (UGIH). Bleeding occurs due to erosion of blood vessels in the ulcer base, commonly involving gastric or duodenal ulcers.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Oesophagitis – Can cause bleeding but is an uncommon cause of significant acute upper GI haemorrhage.

  • Gastric erosions – Can cause upper GI bleeding, especially in critically ill patients or with NSAID use, but less commonly than PUD.

  • Varices – A major cause of severe upper GI bleeding, especially in patients with portal hypertension, but overall less common than PUD.

High-yield points:

Common causes of acute upper GI haemorrhage:

  1. Peptic ulcer disease (most common)

  2. Oesophageal/gastric varices

  3. Gastric erosions

  4. Mallory–Weiss tear

  5. Malignancy

Major risk factors for bleeding PUD:

  • NSAID use

  • H. pylori infection

  • Previous ulcer history

Common bleeding sites:

  • Duodenal ulcer → gastroduodenal artery

  • Gastric ulcer → left gastric artery branches

Pathology-05.question: ৯) GIT secretions contain which of the following immunoglobulin?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is IgA. The gastrointestinal tract secretions contain secretory IgA (sIgA), which is the major immunoglobulin involved in mucosal immunity. It is present in saliva, tears, intestinal secretions, and breast milk.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • IgG – The most abundant immunoglobulin in blood and extracellular fluid; involved mainly in systemic immunity.

  • IgM – The first antibody produced during primary immune response; mainly found in blood and lymph.

  • IgE – Associated with allergic reactions and defence against parasitic infections.

High-yield points:

Immunoglobulin distribution:

  • IgA → Mucosal secretions (GIT, respiratory tract, breast milk)

  • IgG → Most abundant in serum; crosses placenta

  • IgM → First antibody in primary response; intravascular

  • IgE → Allergy and parasites

  • IgD → B-cell receptor

Secretory IgA function:

  • Prevents microbial attachment to mucosal surfaces

  • Provides local immunity without causing inflammation

Pathology-05.question: ১০) Barrett’s oesophagus is a pre-malignant condition of which of the following part of GIT?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is oesophagus. Barrett’s oesophagus is a pre-malignant condition of the distal oesophagus caused by chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD). It involves replacement of normal stratified squamous epithelium with intestinal-type columnar epithelium (intestinal metaplasia).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Stomach – Chronic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia of the stomach are risk factors for gastric cancer, but Barrett’s oesophagus does not occur here.

  • Colon – Colonic adenomas are premalignant lesions for colorectal cancer.

  • Duodenum – Not associated with Barrett’s oesophagus.

High-yield points:

Barrett’s oesophagus:

  • Site → Distal oesophagus

  • Cause → Chronic acid reflux (GORD)

  • Change → Squamous epithelium → Columnar epithelium with goblet cells

  • Risk → Oesophageal adenocarcinoma

Classic association:
GORD → Barrett’s oesophagus → Oesophageal adenocarcinoma

Pathology-05.question: ১১) Which virus commonly causes viral hepatitis?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is Cytomegalovirus (CMV). CMV can cause viral hepatitis, particularly in immunocompromised patients and neonates. It may produce hepatitis with elevated liver enzymes and hepatocellular inflammation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Dengue virus – Can cause liver involvement and elevated transaminases, but it is not classified as a primary hepatitis virus.

  • Mumps – Mainly causes parotitis and can rarely cause pancreatitis or other complications, but hepatitis is not a typical manifestation.

  • Rubella – Causes rash, lymphadenopathy, and congenital rubella syndrome; hepatitis is not a common feature.

High-yield points:

Primary hepatitis viruses:

  • Hepatitis A virus (HAV)

  • Hepatitis B virus (HBV)

  • Hepatitis C virus (HCV)

  • Hepatitis D virus (HDV)

  • Hepatitis E virus (HEV)

Other viruses causing hepatitis:

  • CMV

  • EBV

  • HSV (especially severe hepatitis in immunocompromised/pregnancy)

Exam pearl:
CMV hepatitis is classically considered in immunosuppressed patients with hepatitis-like illness.

Pathology-05.question: ১২) Which of the following is DNA virus?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is Hepatitis B virus (HBV). HBV is a DNA virus belonging to the Hepadnaviridae family. It contains partially double-stranded circular DNA and replicates through an RNA intermediate using reverse transcriptase.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hepatitis A – A single-stranded RNA virus (Picornaviridae).

  • Hepatitis C – A single-stranded RNA virus (Flaviviridae).

  • Hepatitis E – A single-stranded RNA virus (Hepeviridae).

High-yield points:

Hepatitis virus classification:

Virus Genetic material
HAV RNA
HBV DNA
HCV RNA
HDV RNA
HEV RNA

Mnemonic:
"B = Before (only DNA hepatitis virus)" → HBV is the only DNA virus among hepatitis viruses.

Pathology-05.question: ১৩) Which of the following is the most common risk factor for developing HCV infection?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is intravenous drug misuse. Injection drug use is currently one of the most common risk factors for Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection due to sharing of contaminated needles and syringes.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Unscreened blood products – Historically the major route of HCV transmission before routine blood screening, but it is now much less common.

  • Vertical transmission – Can occur from mother to child, but the risk is relatively low compared with injection drug use.

  • Needlestick injury – An occupational risk for healthcare workers, but less common as a cause of HCV infection in the general population.

High-yield points:

Major HCV transmission routes:

  • Intravenous drug use (most common in many regions)

  • Blood exposure (unscreened transfusion historically)

  • Needlestick injuries

  • Less commonly sexual and vertical transmission

HCV features:

  • RNA virus (Flaviviridae)

  • No effective vaccine available

  • High risk of chronic infection → cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma

HCV → Chronic hepatitis → Cirrhosis → HCC risk

Pathology-05.question: ১৪) Amoebic liver abscess is caused by which of the following?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is Entamoeba histolytica. Amoebic liver abscess is an extraintestinal manifestation of amoebiasis caused by E. histolytica. The parasite invades the colonic mucosa and reaches the liver through the portal circulation, producing an abscess typically containing anchovy sauce-like pus.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ascaris lumbricoides – Causes intestinal ascariasis and may cause biliary obstruction, but not amoebic liver abscess.

  • Strongyloides stercoralis – Causes strongyloidiasis, mainly affecting the intestine and lungs.

  • Enterobius vermicularis – Causes pinworm infection with perianal itching, especially in children.

High-yield points:

Entamoeba histolytica:

  • Disease → Amoebic dysentery + amoebic liver abscess

  • Spread → Faeco-oral route

  • Site of abscess → Right lobe of liver (most common)

  • Characteristic finding → Anchovy sauce pus

Amoebic liver abscess vs pyogenic abscess:

  • Amoebic → E. histolytica

  • Pyogenic → Bacterial infection (commonly enteric Gram-negative organisms)

Pathology-05.question: ১৫) Which of the following is the most common risk factor for developing hepatocellular carcinoma?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is HBV infection. Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is one of the most important and common risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) worldwide. HBV can cause HCC even without established cirrhosis due to direct viral oncogenic effects and integration of viral DNA into hepatocyte genomes.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • HCV infection – A major risk factor for HCC, usually through progression to chronic hepatitis → cirrhosis → malignancy. However, HBV is the leading viral risk factor globally.

  • Alcohol – Causes cirrhosis and increases HCC risk, but less common as a global cause compared with viral hepatitis.

  • NASH – An increasingly important cause of HCC, especially in developed countries, but historically and globally HBV remains a major risk factor.

High-yield points:

Major risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma:

  1. Chronic HBV infection

  2. Chronic HCV infection

  3. Alcohol-related cirrhosis

  4. NASH-related cirrhosis

  5. Aflatoxin exposure

Exam pearl:

  • HBV → HCC can occur without cirrhosis

  • HCV → HCC usually occurs after cirrhosis

Pathology-05.question: ১৬) Which of the following is the tumor marker of HCC?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is AFP (alpha-fetoprotein). AFP is the most commonly used tumour marker associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). It is useful for supporting diagnosis and monitoring treatment response, although it is not sufficiently sensitive or specific for screening alone.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ALP (alkaline phosphatase) – A liver enzyme that may be elevated in cholestasis or infiltrative liver disease, but it is not a tumour marker for HCC.

  • CA 19.9 – Associated mainly with pancreatic adenocarcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma.

  • PSA – Tumour marker for prostate carcinoma.

High-yield points:

Important tumour markers:

  • Hepatocellular carcinoma → AFP

  • Pancreatic carcinoma → CA 19-9

  • Colorectal carcinoma → CEA

  • Prostate carcinoma → PSA

  • Ovarian carcinoma → CA-125

  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma → Calcitonin

HCC risk factors:

  • Chronic HBV infection

  • Chronic HCV infection

  • Cirrhosis

  • Alcohol-related liver disease

  • NASH

Pathology-05.question: ১৭) Which of the following are the most common benign liver tumours?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is haemangiomas. Cavernous haemangioma is the most common benign tumour of the liver. They are usually asymptomatic and often found incidentally on imaging.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hepatic adenomas – Benign hepatocellular tumours associated with oral contraceptive use, anabolic steroids, and glycogen storage disease, but less common than haemangiomas.

  • Fibroadenoma – A benign tumour of the breast, not the liver.

  • Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) – A common benign liver lesion, usually found in young women, but less common than haemangioma.

High-yield points:

Common benign liver lesions:

  1. Haemangioma → most common benign liver tumour

  2. Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH)

  3. Hepatic adenoma

Hepatic haemangioma:

  • Most common site → right lobe

  • Usually asymptomatic

  • Imaging: peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in

Exam pearl:

  • Most common benign liver tumour → Haemangioma

  • Most common malignant primary liver tumour → Hepatocellular carcinoma

Pathology-05.question: ১৮) Which of the following is the most common cause of UTI?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is E. coli. Escherichia coli is the most common cause of urinary tract infection (UTI), accounting for the majority of community-acquired UTIs. It originates from the gastrointestinal tract and ascends through the urethra to infect the urinary tract.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • S. aureus – May cause urinary infection, especially in patients with bacteraemia, catheter use, or instrumentation, but is not the commonest cause.

  • Klebsiella – A Gram-negative organism that can cause UTI, particularly in hospitalized patients, but less common than E. coli.

  • Pseudomonas – Usually associated with complicated UTI, catheterized patients, or hospital-acquired infections.

High-yield points:

Common UTI organisms:

  1. E. coli → most common

  2. Klebsiella

  3. Proteus

  4. Enterococcus

Pathology-05.question: ১৯) Anuria is called when less than which amount of urine is passed per day?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is 100 ml. Anuria is defined as the production of less than 100 mL of urine in 24 hours. It represents severe reduction or complete cessation of urine output and may occur in conditions such as acute kidney injury, urinary tract obstruction, or severe renal failure.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • No urine/24 hours – Complete absence of urine (absolute anuria) is rare; clinical definition includes very low output (<100 mL/day).

  • 50 ml – Represents severe oliguria but is not the standard definition of anuria.

  • 500 ml – This is above the anuria threshold and falls within the range of reduced urine output rather than anuria.

High-yield points:

Urine output classification:

  • Anuria → <100 mL/24 hours

  • Oliguria → <400–500 mL/24 hours (adult)

  • Normal urine output → ~1–2 L/day

Causes of anuria:

  • Acute kidney injury

  • Bilateral renal artery obstruction

  • Bilateral ureteric obstruction

  • Severe glomerular injury

  • Acute cortical necrosis

Pathology-05.question: ২০) Which of the following is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in young adult?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). In young adults, FSGS is the most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome. It is characterized by sclerosis affecting some (focal) glomeruli and only parts (segmental) of affected glomeruli.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Minimal change disease – The most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, especially under 10 years, but less common in young adults.

  • Diabetic nephropathy – A common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults with long-standing diabetes, but not the commonest cause in young adults.

  • Membranous nephropathy – A common cause of nephrotic syndrome in middle-aged and older adults, associated with anti-PLA2R antibodies and malignancy/drugs.

High-yield points:

Most common causes of nephrotic syndrome:

Age group Most common cause
Children Minimal change disease
Young adults FSGS
Middle-aged adults Membranous nephropathy
Diabetics Diabetic nephropathy

FSGS features:

  • Proteinuria (often nephrotic range)

  • Hypertension common

  • Reduced renal function may occur

  • Poorer response to steroids compared with minimal change disease

Exam pearl:
Young adult + nephrotic syndrome → Think FSGS.

Pathology-05.question: ২১) Which of the following is the mechanism of developing nephritic syndrome?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is inflammation. Nephritic syndrome results from inflammatory injury of the glomeruli, usually due to immune-mediated damage. This causes disruption of the glomerular capillary wall, leading to haematuria, reduced GFR, oliguria, and hypertension.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Injury to podocytes – Causes loss of the filtration barrier and is mainly associated with nephrotic syndrome (e.g., minimal change disease, FSGS).

  • Scarring – Seen in chronic glomerular diseases and can contribute to progressive renal failure but is not the primary mechanism of nephritic syndrome.

  • Deposition of matrix – Associated with chronic glomerulosclerosis and fibrosis rather than acute nephritic inflammation.

High-yield points:

Nephritic syndrome = inflammatory glomerular injury

  • Haematuria (RBC casts)

  • Oliguria

  • Hypertension

  • Mild–moderate proteinuria

  • Reduced GFR

Nephrotic syndrome = podocyte/filtration barrier injury

  • Heavy proteinuria

  • Hypoalbuminaemia

  • Oedema

  • Hyperlipidaemia

Examples of nephritic diseases:

  • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

  • IgA nephropathy

  • Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis

  • Lupus nephritis

Pathology-05.question: ২২) Which of the following is the most common cause of meningitis?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is viruses. Viral meningitis is the most common cause of meningitis overall. It is usually caused by enteroviruses and is often self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Bacteria – Cause bacterial meningitis, which is more severe and life-threatening, but less common than viral meningitis overall.

  • Protozoa – Rare causes of meningitis, such as Naegleria fowleri.

  • Fungi – Usually occur in immunocompromised patients, e.g., Cryptococcus neoformans.

High-yield points:

Common causes of meningitis:

  • Most common overall → Viral (especially enteroviruses)

  • Most common bacterial cause in adults → Streptococcus pneumoniae

  • Neonates → Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, Listeria

  • Immunocompromised → Cryptococcus

Exam pearl:

  • Viral meningitis → most common

  • Bacterial meningitis → most dangerous and requires urgent treatment

Pathology-05.question: ২৩) Syphilis is caused by which of the following organism?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is Treponema pallidum. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by T. pallidum, a Gram-negative spirochete.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • H. ducreyi – Causes chancroid, characterized by a painful genital ulcer.

  • HSV – Causes genital herpes, presenting with painful vesicles and ulcers.

  • C. trachomatis – Causes chlamydia, lymphogranuloma venereum, and urethritis/cervicitis.

High-yield points:

Common sexually transmitted infections and organisms:

  • Syphilis → Treponema pallidum

  • Chancroid → Haemophilus ducreyi

  • Genital herpes → Herpes simplex virus

  • Chlamydia → Chlamydia trachomatis

  • Gonorrhoea → Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Syphilis stages:

  • Primary → Painless chancre

  • Secondary → Rash (including palms and soles), systemic symptoms

  • Tertiary → Neurosyphilis, cardiovascular syphilis, gummas

Pathology-05.question: ২৪) Which of the following causes radio-opaque renal stone?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is phosphate stone. Calcium phosphate stones are radiopaque on X-ray because they contain calcium, which blocks X-rays.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Oxalate stone – Calcium oxalate stones are also radiopaque (commonest renal stone). Therefore, this option can also be considered correct in a broader context, making the question slightly ambiguous.

  • Xanthine stone – Usually radiolucent because it does not contain calcium.

  • Uric acid stone – Radiolucent on plain X-ray (KUB), though visible on CT.

High-yield points:

Radiopaque renal stones:

  • Calcium oxalate (most common)

  • Calcium phosphate

  • Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate)

Radiolucent renal stones:

  • Uric acid

  • Cystine

  • Xanthine

Exam pearl:

  • Most common renal stone → Calcium oxalate

  • Most common radiolucent stone → Uric acid

  • Phosphate stones → Alkaline urine + radiopaque

Pathology-05.question: ২৫) Which of the following is a feature of AGN?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is haematuria. Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) is a nephritic syndrome, characterized by inflammatory injury of the glomeruli causing leakage of red blood cells into urine.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Proteinuria – May occur in AGN but is usually mild to moderate; heavy proteinuria is more typical of nephrotic syndrome.

  • Lipiduria – A feature of nephrotic syndrome due to increased lipid excretion associated with heavy proteinuria.

  • Hypoalbuminaemia – A feature of nephrotic syndrome due to loss of large amounts of albumin in urine.

High-yield points:

Acute glomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome):

  • Haematuria (RBC casts)

  • Oliguria

  • Hypertension

  • Mild proteinuria

  • Reduced GFR

Nephrotic syndrome:

  • Heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day)

  • Hypoalbuminaemia

  • Oedema

  • Hyperlipidaemia

  • Lipiduria

AGN → Think: Blood in urine + high BP

Pathology-05.question: ২৬) Which of the following causes neonatal meningitis?
Pathology-05.exp:
The most common cause of neonatal meningitis is Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae). Other important causes include Escherichia coli (especially K1 strain) and Listeria monocytogenes.

Among the given options:

  • Proteus – Causes urinary tract infections and occasionally meningitis, but not a common neonatal cause.

  • Haemophilus influenzae – Causes meningitis mainly in unvaccinated children, especially older infants and children.

  • Neisseria meningitidis – Common cause of meningitis in older children, adolescents, and young adults.

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae – Common cause in older children and adults, but not the typical neonatal pathogen.

High-yield points:

Common causes of meningitis by age:

  • Neonate (<1 month):

    • Group B Streptococcus

    • E. coli (K1)

    • Listeria monocytogenes

  • Children:

    • S. pneumoniae

    • N. meningitidis

    • H. influenzae (if unvaccinated)

  • Adults:

    • S. pneumoniae

    • N. meningitidis

    • Listeria (elderly/immunocompromised)

Exam pearl:
Neonatal meningitis → GBS + E. coli + Listeria.

Pathology-05.question: ২৭) Which defective virus causes hepatitis?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is Hepatitis D virus (HDV). HDV is a defective (incomplete) virus because it requires the surface antigen of Hepatitis B virus (HBsAg) for assembly and replication. Therefore, HDV infection occurs only in the presence of HBV infection.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hepatitis A – A complete RNA virus transmitted mainly by the faeco-oral route.

  • Hepatitis B – A complete DNA virus that can replicate independently.

  • Hepatitis C – A complete RNA virus belonging to the Flaviviridae family.

High-yield points:

Hepatitis viruses:

  • HAV → RNA, faeco-oral transmission

  • HBV → DNA virus

  • HCV → RNA virus, chronic hepatitis common

  • HDV → defective RNA virus, requires HBV

  • HEV → RNA virus, faeco-oral transmission

Exam pearl:
HDV = Dependent virus → needs HBV (HBsAg) for survival.

Pathology-05.question: ২৮) Which of the following is the peripheral nerve sheath tumor?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is Schwannoma. A schwannoma is a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumour arising from Schwann cells, which form the myelin sheath of peripheral nerves.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neurocytoma – A tumour of neuronal cells, typically arising in the central nervous system (e.g., central neurocytoma near the lateral ventricles).

  • Neuroblastoma – A malignant tumour of sympathetic nervous system tissue, usually occurring in children.

  • Meningioma – A tumour arising from arachnoid cap cells of the meninges, usually involving the central nervous system.

High-yield points:

Peripheral nerve sheath tumours:

  • Schwannoma → benign, Schwann cell origin

  • Neurofibroma → benign peripheral nerve sheath tumour associated with NF1

  • Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST) → malignant counterpart

Schwannoma association:

  • Vestibular schwannoma → CN VIII involvement

  • Associated with NF2 (bilateral vestibular schwannomas)

Pathology-05.question: ২৯) ‘Oligoclonal Band’ in CSF is a typical feature of which of the following?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is multiple sclerosis (MS). Oligoclonal bands (OCBs) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) represent intrathecal production of immunoglobulins, especially IgG, and are a characteristic finding in MS.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Bacterial meningitis – Typically shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, and low CSF glucose.

  • Viral meningitis – Usually shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose; oligoclonal bands are not a typical diagnostic feature.

  • Tubercular meningitis – Shows lymphocytes, high protein, and low glucose; may have reduced CSF glucose and elevated opening pressure.

High-yield points:

Multiple sclerosis CSF findings:

  • Oligoclonal IgG bands present

  • Increased IgG index

  • Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis

  • Normal or mildly increased protein

MRI hallmark of MS:

  • Periventricular white matter lesions

  • Dawson’s fingers

Exam pearl:
Oligoclonal bands → Multiple sclerosis.

Pathology-05.question: ৩০) Which of the following is the commonest glial tumor?
Pathology-05.exp:
The correct answer is astrocytoma. Astrocytomas are the most common type of glial tumour (glioma) arising from astrocytes. The most aggressive form is glioblastoma (WHO grade 4 astrocytoma), which is the most common primary malignant brain tumour in adults.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Oligodendroglioma – A glioma arising from oligodendrocytes; less common than astrocytoma.

  • Ependymoma – Arises from ependymal cells lining the ventricular system; more common in children.

  • Ganglioglioma – A rare tumour containing both neuronal and glial components.

High-yield points:

Common glial tumours:

  1. Astrocytoma → most common glioma

  2. Oligodendroglioma

  3. Ependymoma

Important associations:

  • Astrocytoma → GFAP positive

  • Oligodendroglioma → "fried egg" cells, chicken-wire vasculature, 1p/19q deletion

  • Ependymoma → perivascular pseudorosettes

Exam pearl:
Most common glial tumour → Astrocytoma
Most common malignant primary brain tumour in adults → Glioblastoma (astrocytic origin
